items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Larry, I played several times, but Larry was into education.

ctx.x: How did Freddie Hubbard and Larry Ridley, two other names I’m at least aware of – how did they factor into this circle?

Finally I met Freddie after I went to live in New York. I actually met him there. That’s when he came to New York, and he didn’t have any place to stay. So we stayed together in my place. Larry, I played several times, but Larry was into education. He was already into teaching at different schools. He was doing more of that than he was playing.
But not during the young days in Indianapolis.

items.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003
items.q: And Billy Fraser, Slide Hampton, all of us, Freddie Hubbard, we all lived in that house.

ctx.x: Yes. So he lived in the house, and she’s like my sister you know. And Billy Fraser, Slide Hampton, all of us, Freddie Hubbard, we all lived in that house. And there was so much music and Yusef Lateef and all kinds of people would come through the house. And Coltrane and I used to go out to Coltrane’s house and hang out with him. I knew him man, I knew this guy. And he was so beautiful and so focused. Sonny Rollins man, Wynton Kelly man, all these guys man, Philly Jo Jones took me on like a little brother, taught…

were a lot of critics and historians that I take issue with because they are not of the same mold like the Leonard Feathers or the Dan Morgensterns. They don’t have the same kind of humbleness and the same kind of commitment. Some woman came up to me the other day because she was very disturbed about what Oscar Peterson said at the gala the other day.
